cards.title: The Foundational Choice: Sync vs Async
cards.teaser: Every communication decision in a microservices system reduces to one question: does the caller wait for a reply? The answer determines coupling, latency profile, failure behavior, and scalability ceiling — before you ever pick a protocol.

runs.text: When Service A needs something from Service B, it faces a binary architectural choice that cascades through the entire system design:

items.text: Synchronous
— A calls B and blocks, waiting for a response before it can continue. The call and the reply are tightly coupled in time. A cannot proceed until B answers — or until a timeout fires.
Asynchronous
— A sends a message and immediately continues. B processes the message at its own pace. The caller and callee are decoupled in time. A does not know when (or whether) B has acted on the request.

runs.text: This choice creates a trade-off between
latency
and
coupling

. Synchronous calls feel simple — they mirror how we think about function calls — but they bind the caller's availability to the callee's availability. If B is slow, A is slow. If B is down, A fails. In a chain of five synchronous calls, the system's availability is the product of each service's availability: 0.99^5 = 95%. Add more hops and availability erodes fast.

Asynchronous communication breaks temporal coupling. A can keep running even if B is down. Messages queue up and drain when B recovers. But asynchrony introduces its own complexity: you must handle out-of-order delivery, idempotency, eventual consistency, and harder debugging. There is no free lunch.

Rule of thumb: use synchronous communication when the caller genuinely needs the answer before it can proceed (a user-facing read, a payment authorization). Use asynchronous communication when the action can complete later without blocking the user experience (sending an email, updating a search index, triggering a downstream workflow).

Sync is a phone call — you wait on hold until someone answers. Async is a text message — you send it and go about your day. One is fast when the other person picks up; the other works even when they're busy.

cards.title: Request/Response: The Call-and-Wait Model
cards.teaser: Request/response is the synchronous pattern where a client sends a request and holds a connection open until the server replies. It is the most intuitive communication model, the most widely used, and the one that creates the tightest temporal coupling between services.

runs.text: In the request/response model, a client initiates communication by sending a request to a server and then waits — blocking the current thread or coroutine — for a response. The conversation has a definite start (request sent) and end (response received or timeout).

This model maps naturally to how developers think about code: call a function, get a result. It is easy to reason about, easy to debug (a request either succeeds or fails), and easy to test. It is also what HTTP was built around: a client opens a TCP connection, sends an HTTP request, waits for an HTTP response, and closes the connection.
The costs of request/response in distributed systems:

items.text: Temporal coupling.
The caller and callee must both be running and reachable at the same moment. If the callee is down, the caller fails immediately.
Cascading failures.
Slow callees slow callers. A 2-second P99 in Service B adds 2 seconds to every upstream caller. In a fan-out — one request that triggers five downstream calls — latencies add up.
Thread exhaustion.

Under high load, callers waiting on slow callees hold threads. Enough of them and the caller's thread pool is exhausted, causing its own requests to queue and time out. This is how cascading failures propagate.
Retry storms.
When a callee recovers after downtime, all the callers retrying simultaneously generate a thundering herd that can overwhelm the recovering service.

runs.text: Despite these costs, request/response dominates microservices communication because it is simple and adequate for most use cases. The problems surface at scale — high request volume, long dependency chains, or strict latency requirements — and are addressed with circuit breakers, timeouts, bulkheads, and retry budgets (covered in later chapters).
Request/response is like ordering at a counter — you ask, you wait, you receive. Simple and familiar, but if the kitchen is slow, you're standing there waiting and everyone behind you is too.

cards.title: REST: Roy Fielding's Constraints
cards.teaser: REST is not just "HTTP with JSON." It is an architectural style defined by six constraints that Roy Fielding described in his 2000 dissertation. Most APIs called "REST" implement only a subset of those constraints — and understanding which ones they skip tells you exactly where they will hurt.

runs.text: Roy Fielding defined REST (Representational State Transfer) in his 2000 doctoral dissertation at UC Irvine. He was describing the architectural style of the web itself — the principles that made HTTP and HTML scale to a global network. The six constraints are:

items.text: Client-server
— separation of UI from data storage. Clients and servers evolve independently.
Stateless

— each request contains all information needed to process it. No session state is stored on the server between requests. This is what makes REST horizontally scalable — any server can handle any request.
Cacheable
— responses label themselves as cacheable or not. Caching reduces client-server interactions and improves efficiency.
Uniform interface

— a consistent interface between components: resource identification (URIs), resource manipulation through representations, self-descriptive messages, and hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS).
Layered system
— clients cannot tell whether they are connected directly to the server or through an intermediary (load balancer, CDN, API gateway).
Code on demand (optional)
— servers can extend client functionality by transferring executable code (JavaScript). The only optional constraint.

runs.text: The constraint most APIs skip is
HATEOAS

(Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State): responses should include links to related actions, so clients can navigate the API without hardcoding URLs. GitHub's API does this — a repository response includes links to its issues, pull requests, and branches. Most enterprise APIs do not. Without HATEOAS, clients are tightly coupled to the server's URL structure, making it fragile to API changes.
Resource modeling is the other discipline REST demands. Resources are nouns, not verbs.
POST /orders
creates an order;
GET /orders/123
retrieves it. The mistake is modeling operations as endpoints:
POST /createOrder
is RPC-over-HTTP, not REST.

Richardson Maturity Model (Leonard Richardson, 2008) grades REST implementations from Level 0 (single endpoint, all RPC) to Level 3 (full HATEOAS). Most APIs in production sit at Level 2: resources + HTTP verbs, but no hypermedia. That is still valuable — just not REST in Fielding's complete definition.

REST is a set of rules for building web APIs that Fielding derived from what made the web itself work at global scale. Most teams follow some of the rules — resources, HTTP verbs, stateless requests — but skip the hardest one (hypermedia links), which is why they call their APIs RESTful but Fielding would not.

cards.title: gRPC: Protobuf, HTTP/2, and Streaming
cards.teaser: gRPC is Google's high-performance RPC framework: it uses Protocol Buffers for typed, binary serialization and HTTP/2 for multiplexed transport, delivering lower latency and richer streaming semantics than REST at the cost of readability and browser compatibility.

runs.text: gRPC was open-sourced by Google in 2015, based on their internal Stubby RPC system. It addresses the limitations of REST+JSON for high-throughput, low-latency inter-service communication. The two core components:

items.text: Protocol Buffers (protobuf)
— a binary serialization format with a strongly-typed schema defined in
.proto

files. Protobuf messages are 3-10x smaller than equivalent JSON and 5-10x faster to serialize/deserialize. The schema serves as the service contract — generating client and server stubs in any supported language.
HTTP/2 transport

— unlike HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple streams over a single connection, enabling bidirectional streaming, header compression (HPACK), and reduced connection overhead. gRPC maps each RPC call to an HTTP/2 stream.

runs.text: gRPC supports four communication patterns in one framework:

items.text: Unary
— one request, one response. Equivalent to a standard REST call.
Server streaming
— one request, a stream of responses. Useful for subscriptions, logs, progress updates.
Client streaming
— a stream of requests, one response. Useful for uploading large datasets.
Bidirectional streaming
— both sides stream concurrently. Useful for real-time, low-latency data exchange (trading systems, game state, telemetry).

runs.text: Trade-offs vs REST: gRPC is not human-readable (binary wire format), has limited browser support (gRPC-Web is a partial workaround), and requires all parties to share the
.proto

schema — meaning schema management becomes a governance concern. Netflix, Cloudflare, Square, and Lyft use gRPC for internal service communication where performance matters. Public APIs remain REST because browsers and external developers need readability.

gRPC is REST's speed-obsessed sibling: it uses a compact binary format instead of JSON and a more efficient transport than HTTP/1.1, so it's faster and supports streaming in all directions. The trade-off is that you can't just curl it and read the output.

cards.title: GraphQL: Single Endpoint, Client-Shaped Queries
cards.teaser: GraphQL, developed at Facebook and open-sourced in 2015, inverts the REST model: instead of the server deciding what each endpoint returns, the client declares exactly what data it needs. One endpoint, schema-typed queries, and no more over- or under-fetching.

runs.text: REST's fundamental tension is that the server defines the response shape. If a mobile client needs a user's name and avatar but the
GET /users/123

endpoint also returns 40 other fields, the client is over-fetching — wasting bandwidth. If a client needs data from users, posts, and comments but must make three separate requests to assemble it, the client is under-fetching — making round trips that add latency.
GraphQL solves this with a query language. The client sends a query describing exactly what fields and relationships it needs, and the server returns precisely that:

items.text: Single endpoint
— typically
POST /graphql
. All queries and mutations go through it.
Schema-first
— the schema defines types, queries, mutations, and subscriptions. It is the contract between client and server, and it is introspectable — clients can query the schema itself.
Resolvers
— each field in the schema maps to a resolver function that knows how to fetch it. A user query might resolve from a database; the user's posts might resolve from a separate service.
Subscriptions
— GraphQL supports real-time data via subscriptions, typically over WebSockets. Clients subscribe to events; the server pushes updates.

runs.text: GraphQL is well-suited for API gateways aggregating multiple backend services, and for mobile clients where bandwidth and round trips matter. GitHub's v4 API, Shopify, Twitter, and Airbnb use GraphQL for client-facing APIs. The complexity cost: query analysis, depth limiting, and N+1 query problems (each user in a list triggering a separate database query for posts — addressed with DataLoader batching). GraphQL shifts complexity from the server's endpoint design to the server's resolver execution.

GraphQL is most powerful as a BFF (Backend for Frontend) layer aggregating microservices into client-optimized responses. Using it for direct service-to-service communication adds complexity without the query-shaping benefit — for that, gRPC or REST is usually simpler.

GraphQL is like going to a restaurant where you specify every ingredient in your dish instead of choosing from a fixed menu. You get exactly what you want in one trip instead of ordering item by item — but the kitchen (resolver logic) has to be more sophisticated to handle custom orders.

cards.title: Comparing the Synchronous Protocols
cards.teaser: REST, gRPC, and GraphQL each optimize for different concerns. Choosing between them is a product of your clients, your performance requirements, and your organizational capacity for schema management. Here is the comparison table.

runs.text: The three dominant synchronous protocols in microservices each occupy a distinct position in the design space:

items.text: REST

— Wire format: JSON (text). Transport: HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. Schema: optional (OpenAPI). Streaming: limited (SSE for server push). Browser support: native. Readability: high. Adoption: universal. Best for: public APIs, external integrations, teams with diverse consumers.
gRPC

— Wire format: protobuf (binary). Transport: HTTP/2. Schema: required (.proto). Streaming: full (unary, server, client, bidirectional). Browser support: limited (gRPC-Web required). Readability: low (binary). Adoption: high in cloud-native ecosystems. Best for: internal service-to-service, high-throughput pipelines, polyglot microservices.
GraphQL

— Wire format: JSON (text). Transport: HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. Schema: required (SDL). Streaming: subscriptions via WebSocket. Browser support: native. Readability: high. Adoption: high for BFF patterns. Best for: client-facing APIs with diverse clients, aggregating multiple services, mobile apps.

runs.text: Common adopter patterns from industry:

items.text: Uber
uses gRPC for internal services (>1000 microservices) and REST for external-facing APIs.
Netflix
uses a GraphQL federation layer (Federated GraphQL) as the BFF for client apps, backed by gRPC and REST internal services.
Stripe
uses REST for its public API — the audience (external developers) values readability and curl-ability over performance.
GitHub
offers both REST (v3) and GraphQL (v4). The GraphQL API handles complex queries ("give me all open PRs with reviews, failing checks, and assigned reviewers") that would require 8+ REST calls.

runs.text: Polyglot communication — using different protocols for different service pairs — is normal and healthy. The anti-pattern is standardizing on a single protocol for every interaction regardless of fit.

REST is readable and universal; gRPC is fast and typed but binary; GraphQL is flexible for clients but complex on the server. Pick based on who is calling and what they need — not on what the team used last time.

cards.title: Event-Driven Communication: Fire and Forget
cards.teaser: Event-driven communication inverts the synchronous model: a service publishes an event describing something that happened and immediately moves on. Consumers react when ready. The producer never knows who is listening — or whether anyone is.

runs.text: In event-driven architecture, services communicate by producing and consuming
events
— records of facts that have occurred. An event is immutable and past-tense:
OrderPlaced
, not
PlaceOrder
. The naming distinction matters: commands are instructions that could be refused; events are facts that already happened.

The producer emits the event and continues immediately — "fire and forget." It does not wait for any consumer to process the event. It does not know which consumers exist. It does not know what they will do with the event. This radical decoupling is the architectural value proposition of event-driven design.
Benefits of event-driven communication:

items.text: Loose temporal coupling.
Consumers can be offline when an event is published; they process it when they come back up. The producer is unaffected.
Extensibility without modification.
Adding a new consumer (a new notification service, a new analytics pipeline) requires no changes to the producer. Open/closed principle applied to services.
Independent scaling.
Consumers scale independently based on their processing capacity. A slow email service can be scaled horizontally without touching the order service.
Natural audit trail.
Events are records of what happened. Retained events provide a complete history of system state changes — the foundation of event sourcing.

runs.text: The cost: you lose the immediate feedback of synchronous calls. The producer cannot easily know if processing succeeded. Debugging requires tracing events across multiple services. Testing requires infrastructure (a message broker). And the system is eventually consistent — different services see state at different points in time.

Event-driven is like posting a notice on a bulletin board: you pin it up and walk away. Anyone who walks by and cares will read it and act on it. You never know exactly who responded or when — and that freedom is exactly the point.

cards.title: Pub/Sub: Topic-Based Broadcast
cards.teaser: Pub/sub (publish-subscribe) is the broadcast pattern: producers publish events to named topics; any number of subscribers receive every event on a topic. Kafka and Google Cloud Pub/Sub are the canonical implementations — and they differ in important ways.

runs.text: In pub/sub, there are three roles: publishers, topics, and subscribers. Publishers send events to a topic without knowing who will receive them. Subscribers register interest in a topic and receive all events published to it. The topic is the broker between them.
Two different models dominate production systems:

items.text: Apache Kafka

— a distributed commit log. Events are appended to partitioned, replicated logs (topics) and retained for a configurable duration (days to forever). Consumer groups track their position (offset) in the log. A consumer can replay events from any point. Kafka is durable, ordered within a partition, and designed for high throughput (millions of events/second). LinkedIn, Uber, Airbnb, and Netflix use Kafka as their event backbone.
Google Cloud Pub/Sub

— a managed push/pull message queue with at-least-once delivery. No consumer offset management; the broker tracks delivery. Simpler operationally than self-hosted Kafka; scales automatically; does not retain messages after acknowledgment. Suited for fan-out to many subscribers with independent delivery tracking.

runs.text: The key architectural property of pub/sub is
fan-out
: one event reaches all subscribers. An
OrderPlaced

event on a Kafka topic can be consumed simultaneously by the inventory service, the fulfillment service, the notifications service, and the analytics pipeline. The order service publishes once; four services react independently.

Kafka's log retention changes the semantics from messaging to a durable event store. New subscribers can read the full history — enabling back-fills, replays, and event sourcing. This is qualitatively different from traditional message queues where messages disappear after delivery.

Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition, not across partitions. If ordering between related events matters (all events for a given customer ID must process in order), partition by the entity key — every event for customer 123 goes to the same partition.

Pub/sub is like a radio station — the broadcaster publishes a signal and anyone tuned to that frequency receives it. Kafka keeps a recording of every broadcast so late-joiners can catch up. Traditional pub/sub systems do not.

cards.title: Message Queues: Point-to-Point Delivery
cards.teaser: Message queues deliver a message to exactly one consumer — the competing consumer pattern. RabbitMQ and AMQP are the canonical examples. Queues are ideal for work distribution: many producers, many workers, each unit of work processed once.

runs.text: Where pub/sub broadcasts to all subscribers, a message queue delivers each message to
exactly one

consumer (the competing consumer pattern). Producers place messages on a queue; a pool of consumers races to claim and process them. This is the classic work queue: distribute image processing jobs, email sends, or report generation tasks across a worker fleet.
RabbitMQ (using AMQP — Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) is the canonical message queue implementation. Key concepts:

items.text: Exchange
— the routing component. Producers publish to an exchange, not a queue. The exchange applies routing rules (direct, fanout, topic, headers) to decide which queues receive each message.
Queue
— holds messages until consumers process them. Durable queues survive broker restarts. Persistent messages are written to disk.
Acknowledgment
— a consumer processes a message and sends an ack. If the consumer crashes before acking, the broker re-queues the message for another consumer. This is the at-least-once delivery guarantee.
Dead-letter queue
— messages that fail processing repeatedly are routed to a DLQ for inspection. Without DLQs, poison messages block queues forever.

runs.text: Queues vs pub/sub: use a queue when each unit of work must be processed exactly once by exactly one worker. Use pub/sub when an event should trigger multiple independent reactions. The choice maps to the semantic of the message: a
task
goes on a queue; a
fact
goes on a topic.

Amazon SQS is the cloud-native equivalent: managed, infinitely scalable, at-least-once delivery. AWS Lambda can process SQS queues without managing consumer fleets — the platform scales consumers automatically.

A message queue is like a ticket machine at a deli counter — customers take a number and wait; clerks call numbers one at a time; each customer is served by exactly one clerk. Nobody gets served twice and no ticket goes unserved.

cards.title: Event Notification vs Event-Carried State Transfer
cards.teaser: Events can carry two levels of payload: a lightweight notification that something happened (consumers must fetch the details), or a full snapshot of the changed entity (consumers are self-sufficient). The choice is a trade-off between coupling and data volume.

runs.text: Martin Fowler distinguishes two event payload strategies in his writing on event-driven architectures:

items.text: Event Notification
— the event carries just enough information to identify what happened and which entity changed, but not the entity's full state. Example:
{ "type": "OrderPlaced", "orderId": "ord-123" }
. Consumers who need the order details must call back to the order service to fetch them.
Event-Carried State Transfer (ECST)

— the event carries the full, current state of the entity. Example: the event includes the order ID, all line items, the customer, the shipping address, the total, and the status. Consumers have everything they need without making a callback.

runs.text: Event Notification trade-offs:

items.text: Small message size — efficient on the wire.
Consumer must make a synchronous callback to fetch data — reintroducing coupling and latency.
If the source service is down when the consumer processes the event, the callback fails.

runs.text: Event-Carried State Transfer trade-offs:

items.text: Consumers are truly independent — no callback needed.
Events are large; sensitive data (PII) may propagate to consumers who do not need it — a data governance concern.
Schema evolution is harder: changing the entity schema changes the event schema, affecting all consumers.
Events contain the state at publication time, not at consumption time — consumers see a snapshot, not live data.

runs.text: Many production systems use a hybrid: carry enough state for common consumer needs (the fields 80% of consumers want), and let niche consumers callback for additional detail. This balances coupling reduction against payload size.

Event notification is a text that says "your package shipped" — you have to go to the website to see the tracking details. Event-carried state transfer is the website email with every detail already included. Convenience vs. data volume — pick based on how often consumers need the details.

cards.title: Smart Endpoints, Dumb Pipes
cards.teaser: Martin Fowler and James Lewis coined this principle to describe the microservices communication philosophy: keep the messaging infrastructure as simple as possible; put intelligence in the services themselves. It is a direct rejection of the ESB pattern.

runs.text: In the Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) era, the Enterprise Service Bus (ESB) was the "smart pipe": a central integration platform that performed message transformation, routing, orchestration, content-based routing, and protocol mediation. The ESB was the brains of the system. Services were thin endpoints that delegated intelligence to the bus.

The problem with smart pipes: they become bottlenecks, single points of failure, and gravity wells that attract business logic. When the ESB contains routing rules and transformations, changing a business rule requires touching the ESB — a shared piece of infrastructure owned by no single team, deployed on its own cycle, and tested end-to-end as a whole.

Fowler and Lewis's microservices principle flips this: services own their logic, their domain, and their communication behavior. The pipes — HTTP, Kafka, RabbitMQ — are dumb: they move bytes. They do not transform, route, or orchestrate. Routing is done by the service, not the network. Business logic lives in services, not middleware.
What this means in practice:

items.text: Services speak simple protocols
— HTTP/REST, gRPC, or plain message formats. No proprietary middleware required to communicate.
Transformation logic lives in the service
— if the inventory service needs to translate an order event into its own format, that translation code lives in the inventory service, not in a shared transformation layer.
No shared orchestration engine

— choreography (each service reacts to events independently) is preferred over centralized orchestration (an orchestrator tells each service what to do). Saga pattern and process managers are service-level concerns.

runs.text: API gateways and service meshes are not ESBs. An API gateway handles edge concerns (auth, rate limiting, routing to the right service). A service mesh handles network concerns (mTLS, retries, observability). Neither should contain business logic. If your gateway is making routing decisions based on message content, you've built an ESB.

Smart endpoints, dumb pipes means the services are intelligent and the infrastructure is just plumbing. The opposite — smart pipes (ESBs) — means your business logic got trapped in the middleware, which nobody wants to touch, change, or test.

cards.title: Polyglot Communication
cards.teaser: A single microservices system commonly uses REST, gRPC, Kafka, and WebSockets — simultaneously. Polyglot communication is not inconsistency; it is protocol selection fitness. The mistake is forcing every service interaction through one protocol regardless of fit.

runs.text: Just as polyglot persistence means choosing the right database for each service's data model (relational for transactions, document for flexible schemas, time-series for metrics), polyglot communication means choosing the right protocol for each interaction.
A realistic e-commerce system might use:

items.text: REST (HTTPS)
— public API for external partners and the mobile app. Human-readable, well-documented, OAuth-secured.
gRPC

— internal high-frequency calls: the product catalog service serving thousands of requests/second from the storefront service. Typed schema, binary efficiency, bidirectional streaming for live inventory updates.
Kafka (pub/sub)
— order lifecycle events fanning out to inventory, fulfillment, notifications, analytics, and fraud detection. Each consumer operates at its own pace.
SQS / RabbitMQ (queue)
— background work: email rendering, PDF invoice generation, warehouse pick-list printing. Task-per-unit semantics, competing consumers.
WebSocket
— real-time order tracking for the customer-facing app. Persistent connection, server-initiated pushes.

runs.text: Each protocol handles what it is best at. The system is more complex than a single-protocol system — engineers must understand multiple paradigms, observability tools must span protocols, and API gateways must route to different backends. But the alternative — forcing synchronous REST for everything, including event notifications — creates unnecessary coupling and fragility.

The governance challenge: polyglot communication requires explicit decisions about which protocols are approved, how they are instrumented, and how contracts are managed. Without governance, every team invents its own communication layer and the system becomes unauditable.

Polyglot communication means using the right communication tool for each job — REST for external APIs, gRPC for fast internal calls, Kafka for events, queues for work distribution. The trick is having clear rules for which protocol to reach for, so the system stays coherent.

cards.title: Service Mesh as Communication Infrastructure
cards.teaser: A service mesh moves cross-cutting communication concerns — mutual TLS, retries, circuit breaking, tracing — out of application code and into the infrastructure layer. Istio and Linkerd are the canonical examples. This is infrastructure automation, not business logic.

runs.text: Every service-to-service call needs the same capabilities: encrypted transport (mTLS), retry on transient failure, circuit breaking on sustained failure, distributed tracing for observability, and traffic shaping for canary deploys. The naive approach is to implement these in every service — using libraries like Hystrix (Java) or resilience4j. This is repetitive, hard to keep consistent, and language-specific.
A service mesh solves this by injecting a
sidecar proxy
(Envoy, in the case of Istio and Linkerd) alongside every service instance. All inbound and outbound traffic passes through the sidecar. The sidecar handles:

items.text: mTLS
— automatically encrypts and authenticates all service-to-service calls. No certificate management in application code.
Retries and timeouts
— configurable retry policies with exponential backoff and jitter, applied uniformly across all services.
Circuit breaking
— opens the circuit when a downstream service exceeds error rate thresholds, failing fast instead of waiting for timeouts.
Distributed tracing
— propagates trace context (W3C Trace Context or Zipkin headers) automatically, feeding Jaeger or Zipkin backends without application-level instrumentation.
Traffic management
— weighted routing for canary deploys (10% of traffic to v2, 90% to v1), A/B testing, and fault injection for chaos engineering.

runs.text: The cost: operational complexity. A service mesh requires Kubernetes (or equivalent), adds CPU and latency overhead per hop (typically 1-5ms per hop for Istio), and introduces another control plane to manage and upgrade. This chapter previews the concept; Chapter 10 covers service mesh design in depth.

Adopters: Lyft (Envoy's creator), Airbnb, and Pinterest use Istio or Envoy-based meshes. The pattern is most valuable at scale — 50+ services — where the consistency benefit outweighs the operational overhead. Below that threshold, a shared library is usually simpler.

A service mesh is like a smart network card for every service — it handles encryption, retries, and tracing automatically, so the application code just sends a message and the infrastructure does the rest. The downside is that you've now added an infrastructure layer that needs its own management.

cards.title: Async Gotchas: Out-of-Order, Duplicates, and Lost Messages
cards.teaser: Asynchronous messaging introduces three failure modes that do not exist in synchronous systems: messages arrive in the wrong order, they arrive more than once, or they never arrive at all. Designing for these is not optional — they will happen in production.

runs.text: Distributed messaging systems make delivery guarantees, and those guarantees are almost always weaker than developers expect. The three canonical failure modes:

items.text: Out-of-order delivery

— messages published in order A, B, C may arrive as B, A, C. Kafka guarantees order within a partition, not across partitions. RabbitMQ and SQS do not guarantee order at all (SQS FIFO queues provide per-group ordering at reduced throughput). If processing B before A produces incorrect state, the consumer must detect and handle it — buffer out-of-order messages, sequence stamp events, or use a total ordering guarantee at the cost of throughput.
Duplicate delivery (at-least-once)

— virtually all message brokers default to at-least-once delivery: they will redeliver a message if they are not sure the consumer processed it (ack lost in transit, consumer crashed mid-processing). This means consumers must be idempotent — processing the same message twice must produce the same result as processing it once. Design for idempotency from day one: use idempotency keys, deduplicate on a consumed-message ID store, or make operations naturally idempotent (upsert instead of insert).
Lost messages

— fire-and-forget publishing with no durability guarantee can lose messages if the broker goes down before writing to disk. Solution: use durable queues and persistent messages (RabbitMQ), or replication with minimum in-sync replicas (Kafka
acks=all
). Transactional outbox patterns prevent losing events when a service crashes after committing to its database but before publishing to the broker.

runs.text: The transactional outbox pattern deserves special mention: the service writes the event to an "outbox" table in the same database transaction as the business operation. A separate relay process reads the outbox and publishes to the broker. This guarantees exactly-once publication from the producer's side.
A fourth gotcha:
thundering herd on replay

. Replaying millions of events after a consumer bug is fixed sounds useful — but if done without rate limiting, it can overwhelm downstream services that assumed steady-state event volume. Always replay with throttling.

Exactly-once delivery is the holy grail of messaging and effectively impossible end-to-end across heterogeneous systems. Kafka offers exactly-once semantics (EOS) within the Kafka ecosystem via idempotent producers and transactional APIs — but as soon as you write to a database or call an external service, you are back to at-least-once. Design consumers to be idempotent; do not rely on exactly-once delivery.

Async messaging has three gremlins: messages arrive in the wrong order, arrive twice, or don't arrive at all. The answer to all three is to design consumers defensively — handle events out of order, make processing idempotent, and use durable infrastructure so nothing gets silently dropped.

cards.title: Choosing a Communication Pattern: A Decision Framework
cards.teaser: No single protocol or pattern fits every interaction. This card provides a practical decision framework — the questions to ask and the answers that point to REST, gRPC, GraphQL, pub/sub, or message queues.

runs.text: Communication pattern selection is not about preference — it is about fit. Ask these questions in order:

items.text: Does the caller need an immediate response to continue?
Yes → synchronous (REST, gRPC, or GraphQL). No → consider async (event/queue).
Is the caller external (browser, mobile, partner API)?
Yes → REST (universal) or GraphQL (if clients need flexible queries). gRPC is rarely appropriate for external callers.
Is this internal service-to-service with high throughput or strict latency?
Yes → gRPC. The binary protocol and HTTP/2 multiplexing pay off at scale.
Does one event need to trigger multiple independent reactions?
Yes → pub/sub (Kafka topic). Each subscriber processes independently.
Is this a unit of work that should be processed exactly once by one worker?
Yes → message queue (SQS, RabbitMQ). Competing consumers; one message, one worker.
Do clients need real-time push notifications?
Yes → WebSocket (stateful, long-lived connection) or Server-Sent Events (SSE, HTTP-compatible, server-to-client only).

runs.text: A pattern summary for quick reference:

items.text: REST
— external APIs, CRUD resources, broad interoperability required.
gRPC
— internal services, high throughput, streaming, polyglot teams with schema discipline.
GraphQL
— client-facing API gateway, diverse mobile/web clients, over/under-fetching is a real problem.
Pub/sub
— broadcast facts; fan-out to multiple consumers; durable event log required.
Message queue
— distribute work tasks; exactly-one-worker processing; load leveling.

runs.text: When in doubt between sync and async, default to async for workflows that span multiple services with state changes. Synchronous chains across three or more services are a reliability risk and should be refactored to async choreography or saga patterns.

Start with one question: does the caller need to wait? If yes, pick a synchronous protocol that fits your audience. If no, pick an async pattern that fits the fan-out vs. single-worker distinction. Everything else is optimization.
